methods.structure:
The function class is LoRA's (an additive rank-\(r\) update \(\Delta W=X\)), but the optimisation variable is the point \(X\) on the fixed-rank manifold \(\mathcal{M}_r\), which is the quotient \((\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}	imes r}_*	imes\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}	imes r}_*)/GL(r)\) of full-rank factor pairs under \((B,A)\sim(BS,S^{-1}A)\); every step is therefore independent of the factorisation gauge. The Riemannian gradient \(P_X(
abla_W\mathcal{L})\) has rank \(\le 2r\) and is obtained without forming \(
abla_W\mathcal{L}\), by differentiating \(\mathcal{L}(W'+Z_1V^{	op}+UZ_2^{	op})\) at \(Z_1=0\) (a rank-\(2r\) LoRA forward and backward pass). The Muon step is the linear-minimisation-oracle direction over the spectral-norm ball restricted to the tangent space, approximated by \(P_X(\mathrm{Ortho}_{2r}(M_t))\); the singular values of this direction stayed in \((0.9,1.1)\) in their runs. Momentum is moved by projection transport and the retraction is a thin truncated SVD (Algorithm 4 also applies a decoupled weight decay \(\gamma\) inside the retraction step), so a step costs \(O((d_{in}+d_{out})r^2+r^3)\) plus one backward pass, as for factor-wise Muon. LOI chooses the starting point whose tangent space captures most of the full gradient. Theorem 5.1 parametrises all maximisers by \(S\in GL_{2r}\) acting on the top-\(2r\) gradient singular pairs (assuming \(\sigma_{2r}
eq\sigma_{2r+1}\)); the experiments use \(S=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha I_r,I_r)\), i.e. \(X_0=\alpha U_{1:r}V_{r+1:2r}^{	op}\), computed by a randomised SVD with \(2(q+1)\) extra backward passes (about 0.25% of fine-tuning time). The paper writes the orthogonalisation as \(\mathrm{Ortho}_r\) although it sets the first \(2r\) singular values to 1; the formula here calls it \(\mathrm{Ortho}_{2r}\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The trained update is a rank-\(r\) matrix in thin factored form, so \(W=W'+X_T\) (with \(W'=W_0-X_0\) under LOI) folds into one dense weight exactly as LoRA does.
methods.identity_at_init: Under LOI the frozen weight is shifted, \(W'=W_0-X_0\), so \(W'+X_0=W_0\) and the model is unchanged at step 0. \(\alpha\) is kept small, which is safe because no Gram matrix is inverted. A variant with LoRA-style zero initialisation is also reported.
methods.key_idea: Optimise the LoRA update as a point on the fixed-rank manifold \(\mathcal{M}_r\) rather than as two factors, so the step cannot depend on the \(GL(r)\) gauge \((B,A)\sim(BS,S^{-1}A)\), and take Muon's orthogonalised (spectral-norm steepest-descent) step inside the tangent space. A matching initialisation picks the rank-\(r\) point whose tangent space is best aligned with the full fine-tuning gradient.
methods.results_note: On eight commonsense-reasoning tasks with Llama-3-8B at rank 16, Riemannion averages 88.1% versus 87.1% for AdamW-trained LoRA, 86.8% for Riemannian-preconditioned AdamW, 86.6% for DoRA, 84.5% for LoRA-RITE and 83.0% for factor-wise Muon.

relations.note: Main geometry-aware baseline (RPrecAdamW, 86.8 vs 88.1). Zhang and Pilanci precondition each factor with the other factor's \(r\times r\) Gram inverse inside an Adam-style update, which keeps a dependence on the parametrisation; Riemannion works on the fixed-rank manifold itself and inverts no Gram matrix.

Both aim at transformation-invariant LoRA updates. LoRA-RITE equilibrates an adaptive update in factor space; Riemannion gets invariance by construction on the manifold. In the paper's Llama-3-8B table LoRA-RITE scores 84.5 vs 88.1.

LOI maximises tangent-space alignment with the full gradient, and the paper states the link to LoRA-GA. Substituting a block-anti-diagonal \(S\) into Theorem 5.1 gives \(U_{r,2r}\Sigma_{r,2r}S_{21}S_{12}^{-1}\Sigma_{1,r}V_{1,r}^{\top}\), which is LoRA-GA's product initialisation (proportional to \(U_{r+1:2r}V_{1:r}^{\top}\)) when \(S_{21}S_{12}^{-1}\propto(\Sigma_{r,2r}\Sigma_{1,r})^{-1}\); the paper itself uses the mirrored member \(\alpha U_{1:r}V_{r+1:2r}^{\top}\). Both shift \(W_0\) by the initial update.

The geometry of rank-\(r\) matrices, here as the \(GL(r)\) quotient of factor pairs. Riemannion does not cite this paper; it runs Muon with the embedded-manifold version of the same geometry (tangent projection, truncated-SVD retraction, projection transport; Vandereycken 2013, Absil and Oseledets 2015).

methods.formula_latex: W_{RP}=R\,W_0\,P,\ \ W_0\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\ (m=d_{in},\ n=d_{out};\ \text{fixed random initialisation, e.g. normalised Gaussian}),\ \ R\in O(m),\ P\in O(n);\ \ y=W_{RP}^{\top}x=P^{\top}W_0^{\top}R^{\top}x\ \ (\text{so in the }h=Wx\text{ convention }W=P^{\top}W_0^{\top}R^{\top}:\ R\text{ acts on the input side, }P\text{ on the output side});\ \ \text{round }k:\ R_k=\Psi_k^{\top}\operatorname{Diag}\big(\tilde G_k^{1},\dots,\tilde G_k^{\lceil m/b\rceil}\big)\Psi_k,\ P_k=\Phi_k^{\top}\operatorname{Diag}\big(\tilde H_k^{1},\dots,\tilde H_k^{\lceil n/b\rceil}\big)\Phi_k\ \ (\Psi_k,\Phi_k\text{ random permutations});\ \ \tilde G=(I+Q)(I+Q+Q^{2}+Q^{3})=I+2Q+2Q^{2}+2Q^{3}+Q^{4}\approx(I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1},\ Q=-Q^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{b\times b}\ \text{(Cayley--Neumann, }k=3\text{; only the strict upper triangle of }Q\text{ stored)};\ \ y=P_k^{\top}\big(W_{k-1}^{\top}(R_k^{\top}x)\big)\ \text{(input-centric: three matrix--vector products)};\ \ \text{every 400 steps (`POET reset gap'): }W_k=R_kW_{k-1}P_k,\ Q\leftarrow0,\ \text{new permutations};\ \ \text{frozen within a round: }W_{k-1};\ \text{trained: the skew blocks of }R_k,P_k\ (\text{embeddings, LM head and norms are trained directly})

methods.locus: Linear layers of Llama-architecture LLMs trained from scratch on C4: Llama-3B for the perplexity tables (60B tokens; 10B for POET-XQ), Llama-8B for the wall-clock curves, and 8B and 13B in the memory and throughput benchmarks. \(W_0\) is a random initialisation, not a pretrained weight. The original POET was also used to fine-tune BART-large (its App. L).
methods.structure: Two-sided orthogonal equivalence: in the paper's convention \(W_0\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times d_{out}}\) and \(y=(RW_0P)^{\top}x\), so \(R\in O(d_{in})\) acts on the input side and \(P\in O(d_{out})\) on the output side, and the weight moves on the orbit \(\{RW_0P\}\) of the \(O(d_{in})\times O(d_{out})\) action, so with exact orthogonality its singular values equal those of \(W_0\) throughout training (the Cayley--Neumann truncation makes this approximate). OFT is the one-sided case \(P=I\). Large orthogonal matrices are reached by stochastic primitive optimisation: each round trains only permutation-conjugated block-diagonal factors \(\Psi^{\top}\operatorname{Diag}(\tilde G^{j})\Psi\) with \(b\times b\) blocks, merges them into the weight after a fixed number of steps (merge-then-reinitialise; 400 steps in the reported runs) and redraws the permutations, so the accumulated transform \((R_K\cdots R_1)W_0(P_1\cdots P_K)\) can range over the full groups. POET-X keeps this algorithm and changes how it is computed: an input-centric order \(P^{\top}(W^{\top}(R^{\top}x))\), so no transformed weight is stored for backpropagation; batched per-block products instead of materialised block-diagonal matrices; permutations as index maps, with two of the four folded into the frozen weight once per round; skew blocks stored as \(b(b-1)/2\) parameters; fused Triton kernels for the Cayley--Neumann forward and backward; and a recomputation variant (POET-X\(_{\text{mem}}\)) that also allows low-bit frozen weights (POET-XQ).
methods.mergeable_reason: \(R_kW_{k-1}P_k\) is a dense matrix of the original shape. Merging into the weight happens periodically by design and at the end of training, so inference uses one ordinary matrix with no overhead.
methods.identity_at_init: \(Q=0\) gives \(\tilde G=I\), hence \(R_k=P_k=I\) and \(W=W_{k-1}\) at the start of every round (and \(W=W_0\) at the start of training).
methods.key_idea: Learn each weight as an orthogonal equivalence transform \(W=RW_0P\) of a fixed matrix, which pins its spectrum, and make this trainable at LLM scale by optimising only permuted block-diagonal orthogonal factors that are periodically merged. POET-X's contribution is the implementation: an input-centric, kernel-fused computation that brings POET's memory down to LoRA-like levels and its speed close to AdamW.
methods.results_note: Pretraining Llama-3B on 60B C4 tokens, POET-X with \(b=512\) (570M trainable parameters) reaches validation perplexity 12.05 versus 12.69 for AdamW and 11.45 for Muon, using 68.5 GB of GPU memory versus 81.0 GB and 70.9 GB.

relations.note: OFT's \(W=RW_0\) is the one-sided case \(P=I\) on a pretrained \(W_0\). POET acts from both sides on a random \(W_0\) and merges periodically; both preserve the singular values of \(W_0\) (OFT preserves hyperspherical energy as well).

BOFT builds \(R\) from butterfly products of permuted block-diagonal orthogonal factors. POET-X uses one permuted block-diagonal factor per side per round and gets coverage from redrawn permutations across merge rounds. The POET-X paper cites BOFT only as related sparse-training work.

Same group. POET-X carries OFTv2's input-centric (matrix-free) computation into the two-sided case, where the gradient for the second orthogonal factor otherwise needs the full weight. The Cayley--Neumann parameterisation comes from the original POET (arXiv 2506.08001) and is shared with OFTv2.

Both pretrain with a parameter-efficient update that is merged into the weight and re-initialised periodically. ReLoRA's update is additive and low-rank; POET-X's is multiplicative, orthogonal and spectrum-preserving.
Memory-efficient pretraining baseline: 14.88 vs 12.05 validation perplexity on Llama-3B (60B tokens).
Baseline: 12.97 vs 12.05 on Llama-3B; in the 8-bit setting Q-APOLLO reaches 20.49 vs 14.78 for POET-XQ.

methods.name: LoRA-Mixer
methods.full_name: LoRA-Mixer: mixture of LoRA experts routed into the attention/SSM projections, with a Routing Specialization Balance Loss (RSL)
methods.paper_title: LoRA-Mixer: Coordinate Modular LoRA Experts Through Serial Attention Routing
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+\sum_{e\in\operatorname{TopK}(p(x))}p_e(x)\,B_eA_ex,\ \ p(x)=\operatorname{softmax}\big(G(x)\big)\in\Delta^{E-1},\ B_e\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ A_e\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}}\ \ (\text{soft fusion over all } E\text{ experts while training the router; sparse top-}K\text{ at inference});\ \ \mathcal{L}_{total}=\mathcal{L}_{task}+\alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{RSL}+\beta\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}}\|\theta_i-\theta_i^{(0)}\|^{2},\ \ \mathcal{L}_{RSL}=\alpha\sum_{i}\bar p_i\bar f_i-\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_x\big[\mathcal{H}(p(x))\big];\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0\text{ (and public or pre-trained experts in the plug-and-play regime); trained: the router } G\text{ (and optionally the experts)}
methods.trainable_params: E\,r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{experts}+\text{a router per adapted projection (about }0.04\%\text{ of LLaMA3-8B in total)};\ 3.88\%\text{ of LLaMA3-8B with six trained experts; router only when frozen public LoRAs are composed}
methods.locus: Linear projections that feed and read out the token mixer: the q/k/v/o attention projections of LLaMA3-8B and Mistral-7B, and the projection layers of the Falcon-Mamba-7B mixer (App. A.11 describes the in-, out-, x- and dt-projections without saying exactly which are adapted). Plug-and-play routing over public LoRAHub LoRAs is shown on Flan-T5, and the LoRA-LEGO comparison uses LLaMA2-7B. The abstract contrasts this with methods that 'primarily' target FFN blocks.
methods.structure: Token-level mixture of \(E\) low-rank deltas on a frozen projection, \(\Delta W(x)=\sum_ep_e(x)B_eA_e\), placed on the attention (or SSM) input and output projections, so the routed update passes through the token mixer in series instead of acting as a parallel branch or an FFN switch. Experts come from three sources: public LoRAs (e.g. LoRAHub modules) kept frozen, independently trained LoRAs, or experts trained jointly with deterministic hard routing by domain label. The router is then trained on a small mixed set (about 2k examples) with soft fusion; inference uses sparse top-\(K\) fusion, and accuracy rises from \(K=1\) to \(K=3\) and then falls in their ablation. RSL adds an entropy term to the Switch-style load-balancing loss. As printed, \(\mathcal{L}_{RSL}\) subtracts \(\lambda\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{H}(p)]\), which rewards high routing entropy and matches the paper's strong-convexity argument, while other passages describe the term as lowering entropy to sharpen routing. A quadratic anchor keeps selected experts near their first-stage weights. The router architecture is not specified beyond its size. The paper writes each expert as \(\Delta W^{(e)}=A^{(e)}B^{(e)}\) with \(A^{(e)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\); formula_latex uses \(B_eA_e\) with \(B_e\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\), the same product with the letters swapped.
methods.mergeable_reason: The routing weights \(p(x)\) change with every token, so \(\sum_ep_e(x)B_eA_e\) has no single static form to fold into \(W_0\); only a fixed, input-independent expert choice could be merged.
methods.identity_at_init: Not identity when composing trained LoRAs: the frozen experts act from the first step and only the router is learned. The paper does not state the initialisation of experts trained from scratch, and the official repository contains only a README.
methods.key_idea: Put a routed mixture of LoRA experts into the projections that feed and read out attention or the SSM, so expert outputs pass through the token mixer, and train the router with a load-balance-plus-entropy loss that needs little data. Off-the-shelf LoRAs can then be composed plug-and-play, on Transformers and Mamba alike.
methods.results_note: On LLaMA3-8B with six experts (3.88% trainable parameters, 48% of MixLoRA's 8.08%), LoRA-Mixer beats MixLoRA on all seven tasks of the main table, for example 65.53 vs 64.44 on GSM8K and 57.32 vs 55.49 on HumanEval.

relations.note: Main LoRA-MoE baseline: top-k LoRA experts inside the FFN. LoRA-Mixer routes on attention/SSM projections with about half the trainable parameters.
Baseline. MoLE learns gating over frozen trained LoRA layers; the paper describes it as close in inference cost but coarser-grained and weaker.

methods.full_name: In-Place Test-Time Training: the MLP down-projection as chunk-wise fast weights with an LM-aligned target

methods.trainable_params: \text{outer loop: the whole model (continual training, AdamW, lr } 5\times10^{-6}\text{) plus } d^{2}+5d\text{ new parameters per TTT layer } (W_{target},\ \text{depthwise Conv1D});\ \text{inner loop: a fast-weight state } d\times d_{ff}\text{ per TTT layer, changed by rank-}\le C\text{ increments, with no gradients stored}
methods.locus: Down-projection \(W_{down}\) of the gated MLP in a subset of layers (every sixth layer, \([0,6,\dots,36]\), in the released long-context Qwen3 config): Qwen3-4B-Base, LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen3-14B-Base as a drop-in, and 0.5B to 4B models trained from scratch.
methods.structure: At inference the only parameters that change are the MLP down-projections of the TTT layers. Each change is the closed-form gradient step of a linear (negative inner-product) loss, so the delta added after chunk \(i\) is the rank-\(\le C\) outer-product sum \(\eta\hat V_{[i]}^{\top}Z_{[i]}\) between the MLP's intermediate activations and an LM-aligned target. The target mixes nearby future-token embeddings through a short convolution and a learned \(d\times d\) map, so the fast weight stores associations from keys to the tokens that follow them; an induction-head argument shows that the next-token target raises the correct logit while a reconstruction target does not. Apply-then-update keeps the scheme causal: chunk \(i\) is processed with \(W_0+\eta\sum_{j<i}\Delta_j\), so the convolution may look ahead inside a chunk. The released code uses a centred depthwise kernel of size 5 confined to each chunk and, by default, the normalised MLP input rather than the token embedding as the target source. Large chunks give parallelism (\(C=512\) to \(1024\) is best in the ablation, 4096 in the released config, whose inner rate is \(\eta=3\)), and inference clips each \(\|\Delta_i\|_F\) to \(\tau\) (\(\tau=10^{-5}\) for all reported Qwen3-4B evaluations). The slow weights, including the new target modules, are learned by ordinary continual pretraining through the unrolled updates.
methods.mergeable_reason: The fast-weight delta \(\eta\sum_{j<i}\hat V_{[j]}^{\top}Z_{[j]}\) depends on the current context and is reset at every document boundary, so there is nothing static to fold; the small target modules stay as extra parameters at inference.
methods.identity_at_init: The Conv1D kernel is zero-initialised (and \(W_{target}\) is a small random diagonal), so \(\hat V=0\) and every fast-weight delta vanishes when continual training starts: the warm-started model computes exactly the pretrained function. At test time each document starts from \(W_{down}^{(0)}=W_0\).
methods.key_idea: Turn an existing MLP's down-projection into test-time-training fast weights instead of adding a new recurrent layer, update it once per large chunk with a closed-form step, and point the update at next-token information rather than a reconstruction of the current token. Test-time weight adaptation then becomes a drop-in upgrade of a pretrained LLM that is compatible with context parallelism.
methods.results_note: After identical continual training of Qwen3-4B-Base, In-Place TTT raises RULER accuracy at 64k, 128k and 256k from 74.3, 74.8 and 41.7 to 78.7, 77.0 and 43.9, with near-equal scores at 4k to 32k.

relations.note: Both let an LLM change its own weights from new information. SEAL writes self-edits and applies LoRA SFT steps inside an RL outer loop; In-Place TTT applies a closed-form update to MLP down-projections inside the forward pass, chunk by chunk, with no backpropagation at inference.

Selective-locus counterpart. Sparse Memory Finetuning updates only the memory-layer slots that a batch activates and keeps the change; In-Place TTT updates a fixed locus (\(W_{down}\) of chosen layers) transiently per context and then resets it.

Both internalise a context into weights. Doc-to-LoRA generates a persistent LoRA from a document with a hypernetwork; In-Place TTT accumulates an additive update to \(W_{down}\) online, of rank at most \(C\) per chunk, over contexts up to 128k tokens and beyond.

methods.structure: A zeroth-order gradient estimate built from \(N\) one-sided finite differences that share one unperturbed loss; to first order it is the rank-\(N\) random projection \(\frac1N\sum_iu_iu_i^{\top}\nabla\mathcal{L}\). The step is divided by the empirical standard deviation of the \(N\) perturbed losses, which estimates \(\epsilon\|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|\), so the update is a zeroth-order normalised-SGD step: large in flat regions, small in steep ones. Rademacher signs turn the perturbed matrix products into additions and subtractions, so the \(N\) perturbed forward passes are fused into one batched kernel (\(1.92\times\) faster on OPT-125M with \(N=8\)). The FZOO-R variant reuses half of the previous batch's losses when estimating \(\sigma_t\).
methods.mergeable_reason: FZOO only changes how updates are computed. In full-parameter mode it edits the model's own weights in place, so there is nothing to merge; in FZOO (prefix) the trained parameters are a prefix, which stays in the input and cannot be folded into the weights.
methods.identity_at_init: Trivial: there is no reparameterisation and training starts from \(\theta_0\).
methods.key_idea: Make MeZO-style fine-tuning converge in far fewer forward passes by averaging several one-sided Rademacher probes per step and dividing the step by the spread of their losses, which turns the update into a normalised-SGD step at inference-level memory.
methods.results_note: Across RoBERTa-large, OPT (350M to 66B), Phi-2 and Llama-3 on 11 tasks, the abstract reports that FZOO beats MeZO by +3% in accuracy with 3x fewer forward passes, and by +5.6% with 18x fewer forward passes on RoBERTa-large (the unit is not stated; in Table 1, \(k=16\), the averages are 71.4 vs 67.4).

papers.title: On the Convergence Rate of LoRA Gradient Descent
papers.claim: For vanilla LoRA gradient descent (\(A\) and \(B\) updated simultaneously on \(\mathcal{L}(BA)\)), assuming only that the loss is \(L\)-smooth and bounded below in the full weight \(W\), \(\min_{t<T}\|\nabla\mathcal{J}(V_t)\|^2=O(1/\log T)\), improving to \(O(1/T)\) if the iterates stay bounded. The factor-space loss is not smooth and the iterates are not assumed bounded. The proof stacks \(V=[B;A^{\top}]\), writes \(BA=E_1VV^{\top}E_2\) (a symmetric Burer--Monteiro form), proves a descent lemma with extra terms up to fourth order in the step, and uses the adaptive step \(\eta_t=\min\{1/(4\sqrt2L(\|V_t\|^2+\|\nabla\mathcal{L}(B_tA_t)\|)),1\}\) together with the worst-case growth \(\|V_t\|^2=O(t)\). The rate has no explicit dependence on the rank \(r\) (only through \(\|V_0\|\)), extends to many adapted matrices by block extraction, and \(V=0\) is always a stationary point of the reparametrised loss.
papers.relevance: The first non-asymptotic guarantee for plain LoRA gradient descent without boundedness assumptions, complementing the landscape result in lora-converges-or-fails-loudly. It locates the difficulty in the reparametrisation: the factor-space loss is only 'Lipschitz-like', with a constant growing like \(\|V\|^2\), so the usable step shrinks as the factors grow. This is the conditioning issue that the gauge-aware optimisers in the catalogue target (riemannian-preconditioned-lora, lora-rite, riemannion, balanced-lora). The stationary point at \(V=0\) exists whatever the loss of \(W_0\), one concrete way LoRA and full fine-tuning can end in different places.

papers.title: Understanding Catastrophic Forgetting In LoRA via Mean-Field Attention Dynamics
papers.claim: In a tied-weight, continuous-depth self-attention model where tokens evolve as interacting particles (on the sphere under Post-LayerNorm) and LoRA is a low-rank perturbation of \((Q,K,V)\), forgetting is measured as drift of the emergent cluster geometry, which the authors correlate with base-task perplexity. (i) A finite-time Wasserstein bound: \(W_2(\mu_t,\nu_t)\le c\,\varepsilon\,e^{c\,e^{ct}}\) for perturbations of operator norm \(\varepsilon\) (Prop. 3.1). (ii) For \(A=K^{\top}Q=V\succeq0\) with a spectral gap and a symmetric update \(\Delta V=\Delta A\), if \(\mathrm{gap}+a>2\|b\|+\|E\|_{op}\), with \(a=u_1^{\top}\Delta Vu_1\), \(b=P_{\perp}\Delta Vu_1\) and \(E=P_{\perp}\Delta VP_{\perp}\), the limiting cluster moves from \(u_1\) to \(\tilde u_1\) with \(\|u_1-\tilde u_1\|\lesssim(2\|b\|+\|E\|_{op})/(\mathrm{gap}+a)\) (Prop. 3.3). (iii) For i.i.d. random rank-\(r\) value adapters scaled by \(\eta_L\) at depth \(L\) there is a norm transition: \(\eta_L\ll\sqrt L\) keeps the mean-square distance to the pretrained cluster at \(O(1/L)\), while \(\eta_L=\sqrt L\) gives a diffusive regime with \(\sum_i\mathbb{E}\|x_i^{\ell}-u_1\|^2\simeq n\sum_{i\ge2}\kappa/(2(\lambda_1-\lambda_i)+d\kappa)\) (Thm. 4.2). (iv) A depth transition: perturbed tokens track the base dynamics up to a critical depth \(T^*\) and then move to a new clustering (Thm. 4.6). Experiments on Qwen3-0.6B show a loss transition in the perturbation norm; rank matters during LoRA training but not for isotropic random adapters, learned updates align with the top direction \(u_1\), and an empirical bifurcation depth moves earlier during fine-tuning. papers.title: Model Merging Scaling Laws in Large Language Models
papers.claim: The expected cross-entropy of merging \(k\) experts into a base of size \(N\) follows a floor-plus-tail law \(\mathbb{E}[L\mid N,k]=L_*+BN^{-\beta}+A_0N^{-\gamma}/(k+b)\), fitted in-domain and cross-domain over 10,866 merged models (Qwen2.5 0.5B to 72B, nine math, science and code domains, \(k=1,\dots,9\)) for Average, Task Arithmetic, TIES and DARE (\(R^2>0.98\)). Larger bases lower the floor and shrink the tail; most gains arrive early (\(k=5\) and \(k=6\) cross 85% and 90% of the nine-expert improvement); the variance across expert subsets shrinks like \(1/k\); and differences between methods compress at scale. A second-order Taylor argument for equal-weight merging (\(\alpha_{i,k}=c/k\)) gives \(\mathbb{E}[L]=L_\infty(N)+A(N)/k+O(k^{-3/2})\), with \(L_\infty=L(\theta_0)+c\,g^{\top}\mu+\tfrac{c^2}{2}\mu^{\top}H\mu\) and \(A=\tfrac{c^2}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(H\Sigma)\), where \(\mu\) and \(\Sigma\) are the mean and covariance of the task vectors. Three early points (\(k\in\{1,2,4\}\)) are enough to forecast the whole \(k\)-curve.
papers.relevance: Gives the post-hoc (P) kind a quantitative law: the return from merging is a curvature-weighted variance term \(\mathrm{Tr}(H\Sigma)/k\) on top of a mean-direction floor, the mean/covariance split that ties-merging, dare and merging-at-scale use informally. The controlled experts are full-parameter fine-tunes (App. D: lr \(10^{-5}\), ZeRO-3; the released OpenRLHF training script passes no LoRA option), not LoRAs; the authors note that LoRA rank and expert capacity would shift the fitted floor and tail, so transfer to adapter merging is plausible but untested.

papers.title: Zeroth-Order Optimization at the Edge of Stability
papers.claim: With the standard Gaussian two-point estimator, the mean dynamics of ZO-GD, ZO-GDM and frozen ZO-Adam near a minimum match their first-order counterparts (critical step \(2/\lambda_{\max}\) for GD), but mean-square linear stability depends on the whole Hessian spectrum. For ZO-GD the critical step \(\eta^*\) solves \(\sum_i\eta\lambda_i/(2(1-\eta\lambda_i))=1\) (with \(\eta\lambda_{\max}<1\)) and satisfies \(2/(\mathrm{Tr}H+2\lambda_{\max})\le\eta^*\le2/\mathrm{Tr}H\), with analogous bounds for momentum (factor \(1-\beta\)) and for frozen ZO-Adam with the preconditioned Hessian \(P^{-1}H\) (assuming \(PH=HP\)). Full-batch ZO-GD, ZO-GDM and ZO-Adam on CIFAR-10 CNN, ResNet and ViT models (and LSTM and Mamba sorting tasks) settle at this mean-square edge of stability, with catapults after step-size increases. Large ZO steps therefore implicitly regularise the Hessian trace, whereas first-order steps regularise the top eigenvalue; large smoothing \(\mu\) and mini-batching push training into flatter regimes.
papers.relevance: The implicit bias of the backward-lens (B) zeroth-order kind behind mezo, agzo, zo-muon and fzoo: ZO fine-tuning is limited by \(\mathrm{Tr}(H)\) rather than \(\lambda_{\max}\), consistent with MeZO's low-effective-rank explanation and with zo-learning-dynamics-kernel. The experiments use small vision and sequence models, not LLM fine-tuning, and the main theory uses MeZO's symmetric Gaussian estimator. Appendix B extends the covariance-operator framework one ingredient at a time: forward differences (with Gaussian directions), non-Gaussian directions (for the symmetric estimator) and multiple Gaussian queries. FZOO's combination of one-sided Rademacher probes with a shared baseline and a loss-std-normalised step is therefore not covered as such, and none of these variants was tested.

papers.title: Riemannian Structure and Optimization for a Class of Low-Parametric Orthogonal Matrices
papers.claim: For Group-and-Shuffle (GS) matrices \(A=B_mP_{m-1}B_{m-1}\cdots P_1B_1\) (block-diagonal factors interleaved with fixed permutations; Monarch and block-butterfly matrices are special cases), explicit counterexamples show that with rectangular or general square blocks the two-factor class is a product of bounded-rank sets and not a smooth manifold. With orthogonal blocks the two-factor class is an orbit of the compact Lie-group action \((B_2,B_1)\cdot x=B_2xB_1^{\top}\) and hence a closed embedded submanifold (recalled from OrthoFuse). For this case the paper derives the tangent-space projection, retractions (exponential, Cayley and polar; the experiments use polar with five Newton--Schulz steps) and vector transport. It computes Riemannian gradients by automatic differentiation without forming dense matrices, covering overlapping block supports and parameter sharing, and gives geodesics under extra block assumptions. It also proves \(\mathcal{A}_3^{\mathrm{orth}}=\mathcal{A}_3\cap O(N)\) and links the three-factor perfect-shuffle case to the CS decomposition. Riemannian SGD on GS-orthogonal adapters (\(b=8\), 1.38M parameters) for RoBERTa-base on GLUE beats Euclidean SGD (84.85 vs 83.12 average) but stays below AdamW (86.04), at 5 to 7% overhead.
papers.relevance: Says when the structured orthogonal groups of the OFT family (oft, boft, GSOFT) are smooth. The two-factor block-diagonal-with-permutation class is a manifold when its blocks are orthogonal (or unitary), which licenses Riemannian optimisation and base-point arguments for GSOFT-style two-factor adapters. The manifold property is proved only for \(m=2\) (for \(m=3\) the paper shows \(\mathcal{A}_3^{\mathrm{orth}}=\mathcal{A}_3\cap O(N)\)), so BOFT's longer butterfly products are not covered, and unconstrained block factorisations such as Monarch (monarch) are not manifolds in general. From the Rakhuba group (GSOFT, OrthoFuse, riemannion). Neither GSOFT (arXiv 2406.10019, NeurIPS 2024) nor OrthoFuse (arXiv 2604.05183, CVPR 2026) is in the catalogue yet.

papers.title: When Can Prefixes Compile LoRA? Exact Resource-Capped Tests for Frozen Attention
papers.claim: At one frozen causal softmax head with fixed content states, and a prefix of independent keys and values shared across inputs, the prefix sees the content only through \(\Sigma(X)=(q,Z_X,N_X)\) (query, partition function, value numerator), and \(\Sigma\) is a complete intervention statistic. Any adapter target that differs on two inputs with equal \(\Sigma\) therefore has an error floor at every prefix length, and with norm caps \(\|\kappa_t\|\le K\), \(\|\nu_t\|\le V\) the floor extends, independently of length, to nearly equal summaries. At a common query \(q_0\) every prefix reduces to two aggregates \((a,b)=(Z_S(q_0),N_S(q_0))\). With \(m\) capped slots the attainable set is \(\{me^{-L}\le a\le me^{L},\ \|b\|\le Va\}\) with \(L=K\|q_0\|/\sqrt{d_k}\), the optimal (projected) error is an attained second-order-cone program, and \(m\) identical slots realise the optimum; with a constant partition, the closure of prefix outputs is exactly \(t\,h_X+c\) with \(0\le t\le1\). Two equal-norm rank-one value updates can fall on opposite sides of compilability, extra capped slots can raise the optimal error, and both query-side and value-side updates can fail. Under affine query exposure, \(2r\) signed slots approximate a rank-\(r\) value update, with values growing as \(O(\epsilon^{-3/2})\); all 400 tolerance checks pass in float64 but only 38 in bfloat16. On three first-layer GPT-2 heads with a fixed readout token, the capped optimum (four slots) leaves 18.4% to 74.2% of a trained adapter's projected effect uncompiled. All claims are local to one head.
papers.relevance: A target-by-target comparison of the prefix (E0) and LoRA (R) kinds that sharpens the indexed prefix theory. It builds on the prefix decomposition of prefix-tuning-capabilities-limitations (Petrov et al. 2024b) and cites petrov-2024-prefix-universal; le-2025-revisiting-prefix and chen-2022-inducer-tuning are catalogue neighbours that it does not cite. A prefix can only mix the frozen head output with a query-dependent vector, so adapters that amplify the frozen output, or that separate inputs with equal \((q,Z,N)\), cannot be compiled. The same authors' 'Certification Frontiers for Gaussian LoRA' (arXiv 2609.32271, PAC-Bayes with KL minimised over the \(GL(r)\) gauge) was posted three days earlier (26 vs 29 September 2026) and was not added.
